title: Probe windowing + fallback experiment log
content:
Purpose:
This doc records a focused set of experiments and design notes around probe-driven windowing for multi-region traffic fallback. The goal is pragmatic: find a small set of heuristics that let the control plane (and clients) react quickly to regional degradations while minimizing churn, DNS churn amplification, and user-visible failures. This is intentionally an "experiment log" — rough notes, hypotheses, results, and follow-ups.

Background / rationale:
- We operate across many regions and support both Anycast and GeoDNS fronts. In practice, failures are often partial (pod-level noise, AZ-wide networking blips, peering flaps) and last 10s-10m.
- We need to balance two opposing risks: slow detection => prolonged customer errors; fast detection => mass reroutes and oscillation (DNS TTL amplification, BGP reconvergence, regional overload).
- Prior docs cover broad steering mechanics; this tries to quantify and tune the probing + fallback time window as a first-class control.

Key concepts we tested (working definitions):
- Probe: a synthetic health check from multiple vantage points (internal agent and external vantage). Probes differ from production telemetry: they run higher QPS and can include multi-step flows (TLS handshake + small payload).
- Windowing: accumulative time window during which we aggregate probe failures before triggering a control-plane action (weight change, ejection, DNS reply change).
- Preemptive rebinding: temporarily returning shorter TTLs and hinting clients to re-resolve during an elevated risk window instead of changing global weights immediately.
- Safe-guard timers: cooldown, hysteresis, and backoff for repeated flaps.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Probing cadence: 5s, 15s, 30s, 60s per vantage per region.
- Failure definition: 3-of-5 probes failed within W window OR 50% error rate in last 60s from production traces.
- Window sizes W: 30s, 90s, 180s, 5m.
- Action types: immediate weight ejection (decrease route weight by 90%), staged partial ejection (decrease by 30% -> 60% after timeout), TTL shortening (from 60s->5s), combined (TTL shorten + staged ejection).
- Recovery policy: linear ramp back over 10m vs immediate recovery when probes pass.

Top-level hypotheses:
1) Short TTL windows (5–15s) + probe aggregation let us move client resolution quickly without global weight flapping.
2) Immediate hard ejection (90%) causes downstream region overload when an upstream transient recovers quickly; staged ejection reduces overshoot.
3) Probe jitter (randomized offsets) reduces synchronized mass decisions from multi-vantage probes.

Test environment and signal sources:
- Vantage points: 8 internal agents (2 per continent), 12 external mimics (third-party probe service), and traffic-sampled client-side health metrics (1% sample).
- Control plane simulator to run rapid sweep tests (see linked PR).
- Metrics: success rate of control action (did it reduce user errors), false positive rate (did we take action for <30s transient), DNS query amplification, regional QPS delta, 5xx user-facing error delta.

Selected results (high level):
- 5s cadence + window 30s + immediate hard ejection: detection latency median 20s, but false positives high (30% of actions lasted <45s and caused >40% QPS variance in failover region).
- 15s cadence + window 90s + staged ejection + TTL shorten: detection latency median 45s, false positives ~8%, DNS churn moderate. Best trade-off for user-visible errors vs churn.
- 60s cadence + window 5m: very low false positives but slow to mitigate; SLA misses increased for brief high-error periods.
- Jitter application (uniform up to cadence) reduced synchronized control plane spikes by ~70% in sim.

Concrete pattern we prototyped (recommended baseline):
- Probe cadence: 15s per vantage; each probe has random jitter ±25% to avoid alignment.
- Failure policy: trigger if 4-of-6 regional internal probes fail across 2 distinct vantage groups OR if production-sampled error rate > 30% in 60s window.
- Initial action: shorten public GeoDNS TTL to 5s and emit a canary weight shift (-30% weight) to preferred fallback regions; keep original region at 70% to allow in-flight sessions to continue.
- Stabilization wait: 90s evaluation window; if errors persist, escalate to stronger ejection (-80%) and keep short TTL for additional 5 minutes.
- Recovery: after 5m of probes passing, ramp weights linearly back to baseline over 10m, then restore TTL to normal.
- Cooldown: after any full-ejection event, block further full-ejection for that region for 30m unless human override.

Why TTL shortening first?
- Changing TTLs is a low-cost hint that nudges new client connections to re-resolve quickly and gives us a softer control path than immediate weight reassignments that can create sudden QPS spikes elsewhere.
- TTLs have variable client adherence, but most modern SDKs respect short TTLs; empirical tests showed 40–60% of new connections honored 5s TTL in first 120s.

Edge cases and discovered failure modes:
- DNS amplification loop: If TTL shortening is combined with an automated ejection that makes the fallback region marginally more attractive, high client re-resolution QPS can surge and trigger our ejection thresholds elsewhere. Mitigation: apply rate limit to per-region weight deltas in a 60s window.
- BGP/Anycast blackhole: Anycast-level blackholes are invisible to DNS-level strategies. Our probe mix must include Anycast-level health checks (TCP probe to same Anycast prefix) to detect BGP blackholes and avoid redirecting via GeoDNS which doesn't help.
- Probe contamination: If probe agents share the same transit path as a failed region, probes will falsely indicate a regional outage. Use diverse transit providers and at least two independent vantage networks.
- Client affinity with long-lived connections: TTL shortening does nothing for long-lived TCP connections; need in-region graceful draining + connection-level hedging (client-side).

Operational notes and runbooks drafted:
- Alerting: create a dedicated SRE alert type for "probe window escalation" with clear runbook links and a pre-filled Terraform toggle to force a global fallback if automation misbehaves.
- Telemetry dashboard: 1) probe pass-rate by vantage, 2) DNS queries per-second per region, 3) weight-change events timeline, 4) failover QPS delta, 5) user 5xx.
- Postmortem template: must include whether TTL reduce or weight ejection triggered, and timelines of probe vs production error divergence.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Should we expose a customer-visible routing hint API (route_preference) to allow enterprises to opt for aggressive vs conservative steering? (security implications + SLAs)
- How to unify Anycast probe signals with GeoDNS decisions in one control loop without circularity? Proposed: centralizing signals in control-plane with a conservative arbitration layer.
- Cost model: measure extra DNS query cost + control-plane churn cost vs SLA improvements to justify defaults. (TODO: run 2-week A/B test with 10% of traffic.)
- Can we use ML to predict imminent regional flaps based on probe derivatives (rate of error growth) rather than threshold hysteresis? (small R&D spike required).

Action items (near term):
- (Ravi) implement TTL-shortening + staged-ejection orchestrator PR (JIRA-PLAT-3487).
- (Ava) add diverse external vantage points behind different transit providers and document probe network fingerprint.
- (Jordan) run 2-week A/B with 10% traffic on the 15s/90s/staged config and collect cost metrics.
- (Simone) update SLO docs and include expected DNS query overhead table.

Notes-to-self / rough heuristics to consider later:
- Always pair any short TTL change with a cap on per-region weight increase rate (limit % of total QPS moved per 60s)
- Prefer staged actions: short TTL -> partial weight shift -> escalate to full ejection
- Use a global random seed for jitter but rotate seed hourly to avoid pathological long-term sync

References / links:
- CONFLUENCE-1221: steering-controlplane-architecture (notes + API sketches)
- JIRA-PLAT-3487: orchestrator for staged ejections and TTL management
- github.com/redwood-inference/steering-sim/pulls/56: simulator code used for the above experiments

Appendix (raw experiment logs excerpts):
- 2025-01-14 03:12Z: simulated cross-region peering degradation in us-west1 -> us-east1 (60s). TTL-shortening-only triggered; observed 45% reduction in user errors and 22% increase in DNS QPS to fallback region.
- 2025-01-18 11:21Z: real incident (peering flap eu-central) where 15s/90s/staged prevented full failover; follow-up: adjust cooldown from 20m->30m.

End of log.

Comments welcome — especially from SREs who own Anycast-level detection and networking teams who can validate assumptions about client DNS behavior.
